case_scope.source_excerpt: Use SI units and an oriented Euclidean three-space with Cartesian coordinates. Here $C^r$ means that coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference body with $C^1$ boundary, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A smooth motion is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times\mathcal U;\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image; when labels are initially the current positions, $\chi_0(a)=a$. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$. For $x\in\chi_t(\mathcal U)$ its inverse label map is $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, and its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$. Position and material-label coordinates have units $\mathrm m$, time has units $\mathrm s$, and velocity has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity gradient is $L=\nabla u$, the rate-of-strain tensor is $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, the spin is $W=(L-L^{\mathsf T})/2$, and the dilatation is $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{tr}L$; all have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The material derivative is $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$, acting componentwise on tensor fields, with units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ on dimensionless fields. Matrix contraction is $S:T=\operatorname{tr}(S^{\mathsf T}T)$, with Frobenius norm $|S|=(S:S)^{1/2}$. These definitions are the mathematical motion and kinematics used below.

citations.quote:
Use SI units and an oriented Euclidean three-space with Cartesian coordinates. Here $C^r$ means that coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference body with $C^1$ boundary, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A smooth motion is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times\mathcal U;\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image; when labels are initially the current positions, $\chi_0(a)=a$. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$. For $x\in\chi_t(\mathcal U)$ its inverse label map is $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, and its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$. Position and material-label coordinates have units $\mathrm m$, time has units $\mathrm s$, and velocity has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity gradient is $L=\nabla u$, the rate-of-strain tensor is $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, the spin is $W=(L-L^{\mathsf T})/2$, and the dilatation is $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{tr}L$; all have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The material derivative is $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$, acting componentwise on tensor fields, with units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ on dimensionless fields. Matrix contraction is $S:T=\operatorname{tr}(S^{\mathsf T}T)$, with Frobenius norm $|S|=(S:S)^{1/2}$. These definitions are the mathematical motion and kinematics used below.

Write $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)=\{D\in M_3(\mathbb R):D^{\mathsf T}=D,\operatorname{tr}D=0\}$. The generalized Newtonian branch is incompressible, so $\theta=0$ and $D\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$. Define the shear-rate scalar $\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2}$, with units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and let $\eta(\dot\gamma)$ be a finite nonnegative viscosity with units $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. The deviatoric stress is $\tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D$, in $\mathrm{Pa}$; no pressure term is included.

Two named viscosity choices are the Carreau form

$$
\eta_C(\dot\gamma)=\eta_\infty+(\eta_0-\eta_\infty)\bigl(1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2\bigr)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $\eta_0\ge\eta_\infty\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $\lambda\ge0$ in $\mathrm{s}$, and dimensionless $n>0$, and the regularized power form

$$
\eta_R(\dot\gamma)=m(\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $m>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s^n}$, $\varepsilon>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and dimensionless $n>0$. For comparison, the unregularized power form $\eta_U=m\dot\gamma^{\,n-1}$ is defined only for $\dot\gamma>0$; its stress is extended by $\tau=0$ at $D=0$. When $0<n<1$, this viscosity diverges as $\dot\gamma\downarrow0$, although the extended stress may remain continuous.

For the Bingham branch use the Frobenius norm just defined, $\mu_p\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and yield parameter $\tau_y\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Its set-valued deviatoric stress graph on $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$ is

$$
\mathcal B(D)=\begin{cases}\{2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|\},&D\ne0,\\\{S\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3):|S|\le\tau_y\},&D=0.\end{cases}
$$

The value at rest is therefore a whole stress ball when $\tau_y>0$. The chosen Frobenius normalization fixes the numerical convention for $\tau_y$; a source using a differently normalized second invariant requires a corresponding parameter conversion.

For the conformation branch, $C(t)$ is a dimensionless symmetric positive-definite $3\times3$ tensor, $G>0$ is a modulus in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\lambda>0$ is a relaxation time in $\mathrm{s}$, and $\eta_s\ge0$ is a solvent viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. Along an incompressible trajectory, adopt

$$D_tC-LC-CL^{\mathsf T}=-(C-I)/\lambda,\qquad \tau_p=G(C-I),\qquad \tau_s=2\eta_sD,\qquad w(C)=\frac G2\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C-\log\det C-3\bigr).$$

Here $\tau_p,\tau_s$ are polymer and solvent stresses in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $w$ is a stored-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The determinant in this formula is positive for symmetric positive-definite $C$, by the finite-dimensional real spectral theorem and determinant multiplicativity. These are mathematical constitutive definitions and adopted model equations. They assert neither empirical validity for a particular material nor existence of a solution to a fluid partial differential equation.

derivations.claim: If $D\ne0$, then $\tau:D=2\eta(\dot\gamma)(D:D)=\eta(\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma^2\ge0$; if $D=0$, then $\tau=0$ and the contraction is $0$.

For finite $\dot\gamma$, the Carreau base $1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2$ is at least $1$, hence every real power appearing in $\eta_C$ is finite and positive; the parameter inequalities make both summands nonnegative.

If $\lambda>0$, the base $1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2$ increases from $1$ to $+\infty$ as $\dot\gamma$ runs from $0$ to $+\infty$; its exponent $(n-1)/2$ is negative for $0<n<1$, zero for $n=1$, and positive for $n>1$. Thus the factor decreases to $0$, is constantly $1$, or increases without bound, respectively. Since $\eta_0-\eta_\infty>0$, adding $\eta_\infty$ gives the three stated limits and monotonicities. If $\lambda=0$ or $\eta_0=\eta_\infty$, direct substitution gives a constant.

Since $\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2>0$ and is finite, its real power is finite and positive; multiplication by $m>0$ proves the regularized viscosity claim. For $\dot\gamma>0$, the unregularized law has $|\tau|=2m\dot\gamma^{n-1}|D|=\sqrt2m\dot\gamma^n\to0$ as $\dot\gamma\downarrow0$, proving continuity of its zero extension, while $\dot\gamma^{n-1}\to+\infty$ when $0<n<1$.

By [F1], $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. Orthogonality gives $(QDQ^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}(QDQ^{\mathsf T})=QD^{\mathsf T}DQ^{\mathsf T}$, so cyclicity of the finite matrix trace yields $D^*:D^*=\operatorname{tr}(QD^{\mathsf T}DQ^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{tr}(D^{\mathsf T}DQ^{\mathsf T}Q)=D:D$. Thus $\dot\gamma^*=\dot\gamma$. Consequently $\tau^*=2\eta(\dot\gamma^*)D^*=Q(2\eta(\dot\gamma)D)Q^{\mathsf T}=Q\tau Q^{\mathsf T}$; the zero-rate extension obeys the same identity.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $u$ be the $C^1$ Eulerian velocity induced by a $C^2$ incompressible motion in Euclidean three-space, and set $L=\nabla u$, $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, and $\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2}$. Here incompressibility means $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}L=0$. For any finite continuous viscosity $\eta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ and the stress law $\tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D$, one has $\tau:D\ge0$. Under a $C^2$ rigid change of observer $x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, where $Q(t)\in SO(3)$, the transformed rate of strain is $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$, so the transformed stress is $\tau^*=Q\tau Q^{\mathsf T}$.

case_scope.source_excerpt: For the Carreau formula $\eta_C=\eta_\infty+(\eta_0-\eta_\infty)(1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2)^{(n-1)/2}$, assume $\eta_0\ge\eta_\infty\ge0$, $\lambda\ge0$, and $n>0$. It is finite and nonnegative for every finite $\dot\gamma$. If $\lambda>0$ and $\eta_0>\eta_\infty$, it decreases to $\eta_\infty$ for $0<n<1$, is the constant $\eta_0$ for $n=1$, and increases without bound for $n>1$; if $\lambda=0$ or $\eta_0=\eta_\infty$, it is constant. For the regularized power formula $\eta_R=m(\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2)^{(n-1)/2}$, assume $m>0$, $\varepsilon>0$, and $n>0$; it is finite and strictly positive for every finite $\dot\gamma$. For the unregularized power stress $\tau=2m\dot\gamma^{n-1}D$ at $\dot\gamma>0$, with $m>0,n>0$, the extension $\tau=0$ at $D=0$ is continuous, even though the viscosity diverges there when $0<n<1$.

derivations.claim: The norm is convex by the triangle inequality and positive homogeneity. For $0\le s\le1$, $|sD+(1-s)E|^2\le(s|D|+(1-s)|E|)^2\le s|D|^2+(1-s)|E|^2$, the second inequality following from $s(1-s)(|D|-|E|)^2\ge0$. Thus $\Phi$ is convex; it is finite everywhere and $\Phi\ge0$, so the supporting-inequality set defined in the Statement is well-defined.

Let $D\ne0$. For every $E\in\mathcal S_0$, expansion of $|E-D|^2\ge0$ gives $|E|^2\ge|D|^2+2D:(E-D)$, while Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|E|\ge|D|+(D/|D|):(E-D)$. Multiplying by $\mu_p$ and $\tau_y$ and adding shows $\Phi(E)\ge\Phi(D)+(2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|):(E-D)$, so the stated nonzero graph value belongs to the set defined in the Statement.

If $\xi$ belongs to the set defined as $\partial\Phi(D)$ with $D\ne0$, apply its supporting inequality to $E=D+hH$. For $h>0$ division by $h$ gives $\xi:H\le(\Phi(D+hH)-\Phi(D))/h$; for $h<0$ the reversed inequality gives $\xi:H\ge(\Phi(D+hH)-\Phi(D))/h$. The identity $(|D+hH|-|D|)/h=(2D:H+h|H|^2)/(|D+hH|+|D|)\to(D:H)/|D|$ and the quadratic expansion in step 1.2 show that both limits equal $(2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|):H$. Since this holds for every $H\in\mathcal S_0$, nondegeneracy of the Frobenius product gives $\xi=2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|$.

At $D=0$, the supporting inequality is $\mu_p|E|^2+\tau_y|E|\ge\xi:E$ for every $E$. If $|\xi|\le\tau_y$, Cauchy–Schwarz proves it. Conversely, if $|\xi|>\tau_y$, choose $E=t\xi/|\xi|$; the inequality would imply $|\xi|\le\mu_pt+\tau_y$ for every $t>0$, which fails for sufficiently small $t$ when $\mu_p>0$, and fails for every $t>0$ when $\mu_p=0$. Hence $\partial\Phi(0)$ is exactly the stated stress ball, proving $\mathcal B=\partial\Phi$ also at zero.

For $\tau_i\in\partial\Phi(D_i)$, the defining inequality gives $\Phi(D_2)\ge\Phi(D_1)+\tau_1:(D_2-D_1)$ and $\Phi(D_1)\ge\Phi(D_2)+\tau_2:(D_1-D_2)$. Adding and cancelling the potential values yields $(\tau_1-\tau_2):(D_1-D_2)\ge0$.
If $D\ne0$, then $\tau:D=2\mu_p|D|^2+\tau_y|D|\ge0$; if $D=0$, then $\tau:D=0$ for every point of the stress ball.

Conjugation by $Q\in SO(3)$ preserves symmetry, trace, Frobenius norm, and the Frobenius product. Substituting $QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ into each nonzero formula therefore gives $Q\tau Q^{\mathsf T}$; at $D=0$, the full ball maps onto itself because $|Q\tau Q^{\mathsf T}|=|\tau|$. This proves the stated rotation-equivariance.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Define the Bingham graph by $\mathcal B(D)=\{2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|\}$ when $D\ne0$, and by $\mathcal B(0)=\{\tau\in\mathcal S_0:|\tau|\le\tau_y\}$ when $D=0$; its graph stresses are in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Then $\Phi$ is finite, nonnegative, and convex; $\mathcal B(D)=\partial\Phi(D)$ for every $D$; the graph is monotone in the sense that $(\tau_1-\tau_2):(D_1-D_2)\ge0$ whenever $\tau_i\in\mathcal B(D_i)$; every graph value satisfies $\tau:D\ge0$; and, for $Q\in SO(3)$, $\mathcal B(QDQ^{\mathsf T})=Q\mathcal B(D)Q^{\mathsf T}$.

citations.quote:
Use SI units and an oriented Euclidean three-space with Cartesian coordinates. Here $C^r$ means that coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference body with $C^1$ boundary, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A smooth motion is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times\mathcal U;\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image; when labels are initially the current positions, $\chi_0(a)=a$. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$. For $x\in\chi_t(\mathcal U)$ its inverse label map is $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, and its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$. Position and material-label coordinates have units $\mathrm m$, time has units $\mathrm s$, and velocity has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity gradient is $L=\nabla u$, the rate-of-strain tensor is $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, the spin is $W=(L-L^{\mathsf T})/2$, and the dilatation is $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{tr}L$; all have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The material derivative is $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$, acting componentwise on tensor fields, with units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ on dimensionless fields. Matrix contraction is $S:T=\operatorname{tr}(S^{\mathsf T}T)$, with Frobenius norm $|S|=(S:S)^{1/2}$. These definitions are the mathematical motion and kinematics used below.

Write $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)=\{D\in M_3(\mathbb R):D^{\mathsf T}=D,\operatorname{tr}D=0\}$. The generalized Newtonian branch is incompressible, so $\theta=0$ and $D\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$. Define the shear-rate scalar $\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2}$, with units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and let $\eta(\dot\gamma)$ be a finite nonnegative viscosity with units $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. The deviatoric stress is $\tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D$, in $\mathrm{Pa}$; no pressure term is included.

Two named viscosity choices are the Carreau form

$$
\eta_C(\dot\gamma)=\eta_\infty+(\eta_0-\eta_\infty)\bigl(1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2\bigr)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $\eta_0\ge\eta_\infty\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $\lambda\ge0$ in $\mathrm{s}$, and dimensionless $n>0$, and the regularized power form

$$
\eta_R(\dot\gamma)=m(\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $m>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s^n}$, $\varepsilon>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and dimensionless $n>0$. For comparison, the unregularized power form $\eta_U=m\dot\gamma^{\,n-1}$ is defined only for $\dot\gamma>0$; its stress is extended by $\tau=0$ at $D=0$. When $0<n<1$, this viscosity diverges as $\dot\gamma\downarrow0$, although the extended stress may remain continuous.

For the Bingham branch use the Frobenius norm just defined, $\mu_p\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and yield parameter $\tau_y\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Its set-valued deviatoric stress graph on $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$ is

$$
\mathcal B(D)=\begin{cases}\{2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|\},&D\ne0,\\\{S\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3):|S|\le\tau_y\},&D=0.\end{cases}
$$

The value at rest is therefore a whole stress ball when $\tau_y>0$. The chosen Frobenius normalization fixes the numerical convention for $\tau_y$; a source using a differently normalized second invariant requires a corresponding parameter conversion.

For the conformation branch, $C(t)$ is a dimensionless symmetric positive-definite $3\times3$ tensor, $G>0$ is a modulus in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\lambda>0$ is a relaxation time in $\mathrm{s}$, and $\eta_s\ge0$ is a solvent viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. Along an incompressible trajectory, adopt

$$D_tC-LC-CL^{\mathsf T}=-(C-I)/\lambda,\qquad \tau_p=G(C-I),\qquad \tau_s=2\eta_sD,\qquad w(C)=\frac G2\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C-\log\det C-3\bigr).$$

Here $\tau_p,\tau_s$ are polymer and solvent stresses in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $w$ is a stored-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The determinant in this formula is positive for symmetric positive-definite $C$, by the finite-dimensional real spectral theorem and determinant multiplicativity. These are mathematical constitutive definitions and adopted model equations. They assert neither empirical validity for a particular material nor existence of a solution to a fluid partial differential equation.

derivations.claim: Since $u$ and $x$ are $C^1$, $L(t)=\nabla u(t,x(t))$ is continuous on the compact interval $[0,T]$. Applying [F1] gives a unique $C^1$ solution $Z'=LZ$, $Z(0)=I$ on all of $[0,T]$; by [F2], each $Z(t)$ is invertible.
By [F3] and the chain rule along $Z$, $(Z^{-1})'=-Z^{-1}Z'Z^{-1}=-Z^{-1}L$; transposing gives $(Z^{-\mathsf T})'=-L^{\mathsf T}Z^{-\mathsf T}$.

Define $Y(t)=e^{t/\lambda}Z(t)^{-1}C(t)Z(t)^{-\mathsf T}$. Product differentiation using [F4], then substitution of the equation for $C'$ and the identities in step 2.1, cancels the $LC$ and $CL^{\mathsf T}$ terms and yields $Y'(t)=\frac1\lambda e^{t/\lambda}Z(t)^{-1}Z(t)^{-\mathsf T}$.

Since $Y(0)=C_0$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $Y(t)=C_0+\frac1\lambda\int_0^t e^{s/\lambda}Z(s)^{-1}Z(s)^{-\mathsf T}\,ds$. For nonzero $v$, the integrand's quadratic form is $e^{s/\lambda}|Z(s)^{-\mathsf T}v|^2/\lambda>0$; its integral is positive semidefinite (zero at $t=0$), so adding it to the positive-definite $C_0$ makes $Y(t)$ positive definite for every $t\in[0,T]$. The identity $C=e^{-t/\lambda}ZYZ^{\mathsf T}$ and invertibility of $Z$ then give $v^{\mathsf T}Cv=e^{-t/\lambda}(Z^{\mathsf T}v)^{\mathsf T}Y(Z^{\mathsf T}v)>0$ for every nonzero $v$.

By [F10], a material trajectory transforms with velocity $u^*=Q'x+Qu+c'$ and gradient $L^*=QLQ^{\mathsf T}+Q'Q^{\mathsf T}$. Along that trajectory, differentiating $C^*=QCQ^{\mathsf T}$ by the chain and product rules gives $D_t^*C^*=Q(D_tC)Q^{\mathsf T}+Q'CQ^{\mathsf T}+QCQ'^{\mathsf T}$. Substituting these formulas cancels the observer-derivative terms and gives $D_t^*C^*-L^*C^*-C^*(L^*)^{\mathsf T}=Q(D_tC-LC-CL^{\mathsf T})Q^{\mathsf T}$. Since $C^*-I=Q(C-I)Q^{\mathsf T}$, the conformation equation is covariant.

By [F6], write $C=Q\operatorname{diag}(c_1,c_2,c_3)Q^{\mathsf T}$ with $c_i>0$. Determinant multiplicativity and $QQ^{\mathsf T}=I$ give $\det C=c_1c_2c_3$; finite-sum trace cyclicity gives $\operatorname{tr}C=\sum_i c_i$; hence [F7] gives $\log\det C=\sum_i\log c_i$. For each $c>0$, [F5] gives $\log c=\int_1^c dt/t$: if $c>1$, then $\log c<c-1$ because $1/t<1$ on the interior of $[1,c]$; if $0<c<1$, then $\log c=-\int_c^1dt/t<-(1-c)=c-1$ because $1/t>1$ on the interior of $[c,1]$; at $c=1$ the integral is zero. Thus $c-\log c-1\ge0$, with equality exactly at $c=1$, so $w(C)=\frac G2\sum_i(c_i-\log c_i-1)\ge0$, with equality exactly when all $c_i=1$, that is, $C=I$.

By [F6], write $C=U\operatorname{diag}(c_1,c_2,c_3)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $c_i>0$. The unique positive square root and inverse square root in [F8] are $U\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{c_i})U^{\mathsf T}$ and $U\operatorname{diag}(c_i^{-1/2})U^{\mathsf T}$, respectively. Thus $C^{-1}=U\operatorname{diag}(c_i^{-1})U^{\mathsf T}$ and $\operatorname{tr}C+\operatorname{tr}C^{-1}-6=\sum_{i=1}^3(c_i+c_i^{-1}-2)=\sum_{i=1}^3(\sqrt{c_i}-c_i^{-1/2})^2\ge0$.

Since $C$ is positive definite by step 4.1 and $\det C>0$ by step 5.1, Jacobi's formula and the derivative of logarithm in [F5] give $\frac{d}{dt}w(C)=\frac G2\operatorname{tr}((I-C^{-1})C')$. Substituting [A1] and multiplying out gives
$\operatorname{tr}((I-C^{-1})(LC+CL^{\mathsf T}))=\operatorname{tr}(LC)+\operatorname{tr}(CL^{\mathsf T})-\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}LC)-\operatorname{tr}(L^{\mathsf T})$.
The finite-sum identity $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ and $C^{\mathsf T}=C$ give $\operatorname{tr}(CL^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{tr}(LC)$, $\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}LC)=\operatorname{tr}L$, and $\operatorname{tr}(L^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{tr}L$. Also $(C-I):D=\operatorname{tr}((C-I)L)=\operatorname{tr}(LC)-\operatorname{tr}L$, since the contraction of a symmetric matrix with the skew part of $L$ is zero. Therefore the displayed linear term is $2(C-I):D$. Direct multiplication gives $(I-C^{-1})(C-I)=C+C^{-1}-2I$, so its trace is $\operatorname{tr}C+\operatorname{tr}C^{-1}-6$. Hence $\frac{d}{dt}w=G(C-I):D-\frac{G}{2\lambda}(\operatorname{tr}C+\operatorname{tr}C^{-1}-6)$.

From [A1], $(\tau_s+\tau_p):D=2\eta_sD:D+G(C-I):D$. Subtracting the derivative in step 5.1 gives the identity in the Statement; it is nonnegative by $\eta_s\ge0$, $D:D\ge0$, and step 5.2. Since $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ and $C^*=QCQ^{\mathsf T}$, the stress definitions give $\tau_s^*=Q\tau_sQ^{\mathsf T}$ and $\tau_p^*=Q\tau_pQ^{\mathsf T}$; trace and determinant invariance give $w(C^*)=w(C)$.
